issues.legal_issue: A court may grant ejectment on the basis of permissive possession even when the pleaded tenancy is not proved, if the licence issue was in substance tried and the parties had an opportunity to present evidence on it.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership and sought ejectment on the basis of a tenancy, while the defendant admitted the plaintiff’s title to the land and said he occupied the house with the plaintiff’s permission until construction costs were repaid.
The parties led evidence on the plaintiff’s tenancy claim and the defendant’s account of the terms on which he entered possession.
The trial court disbelieved the defendant’s account, and the High Court found the tenancy claim unproved but treated the defendant as a licensee.
The defendant did not identify any plea he could have raised or evidence he was prevented from presenting if licence had been expressly pleaded.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could confirm the ejectment decree on the basis that the defendant was a licensee; the defendant’s appeal against ejectment was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Relief ordinarily must rest on the pleadings and issues, and a party cannot sustain a claim on an entirely new ground that was neither raised nor tried. But the substance of the trial prevails over a formal defect in pleadings where the issue was in substance before the parties, both sides knew it was involved and had an opportunity to lead evidence, and allowing reliance on it causes no prejudice. The Court applied the principles in Trojan & Co. Ltd. v. Rm. N. N. Nagappa Chettiar, [1953] S.C.R. 789, and Sheodhar Rai v. Suraj Prasad Singh, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 758, distinguishing them because the alternative ground here was in substance covered by the parties’ cases and evidence. It also referred to Abdul Ghani v. Musammat Babni and Balmakund v. Dalu.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and owner_title_admitted and permissive_possession_admitted and tenancy_and_condition_claims_tried and both_parties_had_opportunity_to_present_evidence

predicates.ejectment_suit: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking to recover possession of property from its occupant.
predicates.owner_title_admitted: The occupant acknowledged the claimant’s ownership of the property or the underlying land.
predicates.permissive_possession_admitted: The occupant’s account of possession treated entry or continued occupation as permitted by the claimant, subject to a stated condition.
predicates.tenancy_and_condition_claims_tried: The parties presented competing accounts of whether occupation was a tenancy or permissive possession subject to a condition.
predicates.both_parties_had_opportunity_to_present_: Both parties knew the relevant possession issue was involved in the trial and had an opportunity to present evidence about it.

issues.definition: When an ejectment suit involves admitted ownership and permissive possession, and both sides tried the competing accounts with an opportunity to present evidence, ejectment may be granted on the basis of a licence.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for past rent cannot be sustained when the alleged tenancy and its terms are unproved and the required permission for letting was absent.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought past rent on the basis of an alleged tenancy.
The courts did not accept the plaintiff’s account of the tenancy or establish its terms.

The High Court found that the relevant law required permission from the District Magistrate or another appropriate authority before premises could be let, and that the alleged tenancy would have been invalid even if proved.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s rejection of the claim for past rent.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the claim for past rent was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with the rejection of past rent where the alleged tenancy and its terms had not been established. It noted the applicable U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, and the preceding ordinance, which required permission from the District Magistrate or another appropriate authority before premises could be let.

predicates.past_rent_claim_in_ejectment_suit: A claimant sought past rent in a suit also seeking to recover possession of property.
predicates.tenancy_terms_unproved: The claimant did not establish the alleged tenancy and its terms.
predicates.required_letting_permission_absent: The permission required for letting the premises was not obtained.

issues.definition: When past rent is claimed in an ejectment suit but the tenancy terms are unproved and required letting permission is absent, the past-rent claim is not awarded.

issues.legal_issue: An ejectment decree for an occupant who remains in possession must provide for mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the decree until delivery of possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff became entitled to ejectment of the defendant.
The defendant remained in possession after the ejectment decree.
The High Court had rejected the claim for future mesne profits, but the Supreme Court held that the ejectment decree could not stand without a direction covering post-decree occupation.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was awarded future mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the date of the trial court’s ejectment decree until delivery of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Once a claimant is entitled to ejectment, an occupant who remains in possession after the decree must pay mesne profits or damages for use and occupation until possession is delivered. An ejectment decree in those circumstances must include a direction for that payment.

predicates.ejectment_decree_awarded: The court granted a decree requiring the occupant to give up possession of the property.
predicates.occupant_remains_in_possession_after_dec: The occupant continued to hold the property after the ejectment decree.

issues.definition: When an ejectment decree is granted and the occupant remains in possession afterward, compensation for post-decree occupation is awarded.
